name: Skin whitening/bleaching
summary: Lightening skin tone with topical agents, supplements or injections, discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to raise appearance scores; the practice is long-established worldwide and carries well-documented risks.
lead: Skin whitening, also called skin lightening or bleaching, is the use of chemical substances to lighten skin color or even out tone by reducing melanin. Recorded practices date back more than two thousand years, and use is widespread across Africa, Asia and elsewhere.
claims: Lightening skin adds about 0.5 to 1 PSL.
Kojic acid, arbutin and hydroquinone products can lighten skin.
Glutathione (oral or injected) lightens skin.
Mercury or steroid-containing creams lighten skin.

name: Pheromone cologne
summary: Scents sold with the claim that added pheromones make the wearer more attractive; reviewers say no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior.
lead: Pheromone cologne is a perfume or body spray marketed with the claim that it contains human pheromones that make the wearer more sexually attractive. Wikipedia reports that such claims are unsupported by peer-reviewed evidence.

name: Frenotomy / tongue tie release for face
summary: Surgical release of the tongue's frenulum, discussed online as a step toward better tongue posture and jaw development; studies cover feeding and speech, not facial appearance.
lead: Frenotomy, also called frenectomy or frenuloplasty, is the surgical release of the lingual frenulum in people with tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). It is established for some infants with breastfeeding difficulty, and its use for speech, sleep and other outcomes is debated.

name: Face rating apps / AI scoring
summary: Apps and AI tools that score a face photo for attractiveness, popular in looksmaxxing; the scores are model outputs, and a notable early contest drew bias complaints.
lead: Face rating apps and AI scoring tools estimate a person's attractiveness from a photograph and return a number or tier. In looksmaxxing they are used alongside forum ratings and paid analyses by content creators, and some report results on community scales such as PSL.

name: PSL scale
summary: The community rating system, roughly 1 to 8, for male facial attractiveness; it is informal and not scientifically validated.
lead: The PSL scale, short for Perceived Sexual Levels, is an informal system for rating male facial attractiveness on roughly a 1 to 8 range. Wikipedia reports it was created on three forums, PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, whose initials form the acronym; the forums are defunct but the terminology spread to wider social media.
claims: PSL measures facial attractiveness as women perceive it.
PSL and appeal are different things.

name: Canthal tilt theory
summary: The idea that the upward or downward angle of the eye corners drives how attractive a face is; the angle is real and measurable, the strong rule built on it is not well studied.
lead: Canthal tilt is the angle between a horizontal line and the line joining the inner corner (medial canthus) and outer corner (lateral canthus) of the eye. In looksmaxxing slang a positive tilt means the outer corner sits higher than the inner corner, a neutral tilt means they are level, and a negative tilt means the outer corner sits lower.
claims: A positive canthal tilt is a key marker of male attractiveness.
Mewing or tongue posture can raise canthal tilt by moving the upper jaw and cheeks.
Tilt cannot be changed without surgery.
A negative canthal tilt makes a man's outcomes hopeless.

name: Hunter eyes
summary: A looksmaxxing label for deep-set, slightly hooded eyes with an upward tilt; popular as an ideal online, with no formal medical definition and little direct research.
lead: Hunter eyes is an informal looksmaxxing term for an eye area said to look intense and masculine. Descriptions generally include a positive canthal tilt, deep-set eyes, limited upper-eyelid exposure and low-set eyebrows. The opposite is called 'prey eyes', described as rounder and showing more sclera with a negative tilt.
claims: Hunter eyes are a top-tier attractive trait.
Hunter eyes can be trained with exercises or squinting.
Hunter eyes are overrated or a meme.

name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)
summary: Cheekbone width divided by upper-face height; real research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression, and forums treat it as a masculinity and attractiveness score.
lead: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR or fWHR) is the distance between the cheekbones (bizygomatic width) divided by the height of the upper face, typically measured between the upper lip and the brow. It is a size-independent measure and has been studied as a possible sexually dimorphic cue linked to dominance, threat and aggression.
claims: A high FWHR signals masculinity and dominance.
FWHR is a precise number that can be measured from any photo.
FWHR is set by prenatal or pubertal testosterone.

name: Golden ratio face analysis
summary: Judging a face by how closely its proportions match phi (about 1.618) or a set of ideal ratios; popular in forums, with research finding little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness.
lead: Golden ratio face analysis is the practice of measuring facial proportions and comparing them with ideal values, most famously the golden ratio phi, about 1.618. In looksmaxxing forums the analyses are posted as lists of ratios, for example mouth-to-nose width, eye spacing and midface proportions, with each labelled ideal or off.
claims: A face whose proportions match ideal ratios is more attractive.
Ratio scores can be calculated precisely enough to guide decisions.

name: Mogging / AMOG
summary: Looksmaxxing slang for outshining another man in appearance, from 'AMOG'; a social concept with no research of its own.
lead: Mogging is looksmaxxing slang for asserting dominance or superiority over another person on the basis of appearance, outshining them in looks or in a particular trait. The word is generally said to come from AMOG, short for 'alpha male of the group'.
claims: Being mogged lowers how attractive you appear in a given setting.
Height or face can be compensated for by other traits, so mogging can be avoided.

name: Black pill ideology
summary: The incel-originated belief that genetics and looks largely fix a man's romantic and social outcomes; studied by researchers mainly for its links to mental-health burden and misogynistic extremism.
lead: The black pill is a belief system associated with online incel (involuntary celibate) communities. Wikipedia describes it as a more nihilistic offshoot of the red pill idea, holding that dating and society mainly benefit women and physically attractive men and that unattractive men cannot escape this hierarchy because success is set by genetics. The pill metaphor comes from The Matrix.
claims: Looks and genetics largely determine a man's romantic and social outcomes.
Because looks are fixed, improvement efforts are pointless.
Blackpill belief harms mental health.

name: Halo effect
summary: The bias where one good trait, usually looks, colors how everything else about you is judged; well documented in psychology, central to looksmaxxing talk.
lead: The halo effect is a cognitive bias in which an overall positive impression of a person, brand or product in one area shapes judgments in other, unrelated areas. The term is credited to the psychologist Edward Thorndike, who in 1920 reported that military officers' ratings of their soldiers on separate qualities were suspiciously correlated, as if a general impression were coloring each specific judgment.
claims: Good-looking people are believed more and judged less harshly.
Forum users rate content by the poster's looks rather than the content.
The halo makes attractive people succeed everywhere, from school to jobs.
Height, hair or frame create their own 'halos'.

name: Sexual market value (SMV)
summary: A manosphere and looksmaxxing term for a person's overall desirability as a partner, roughly the community cousin of academic 'mate value' and 'sexual capital' ideas.
lead: Sexual market value, usually abbreviated SMV, is a term used mainly in manosphere, pick-up artist and looksmaxxing communities for a person's overall desirability as a sexual or romantic partner. It treats dating as a market in which individuals have a comparable value that determines the partners they can attract.
claims: Looks are the dominant component of a man's SMV.
Facial and body features can be changed to raise SMV.
Race strongly shapes SMV, with tier lists of groups.
Perceptions of one's own SMV are distorted.

name: Jestermaxxing
summary: Forum slang for using clowning and humor to win social and romantic attention when looks alone aren't enough; research on humor and attraction exists, but not on the term.
lead: Jestermaxxing is a slang term in looksmaxxing communities for using humor, clowning or entertaining behavior to gain social acceptance or romantic interest. The word combines 'jester' with the '-maxxing' suffix used for optimization practices in these communities.
claims: Humor and clowning let less attractive men attract women.
It fails if you look unattractive or seem desperate.
Jestermaxxing and slaying are cope; authenticity works better.

name: Looksmatching
summary: Forum term for couples paired at a similar attractiveness level, the community version of the psychology 'matching hypothesis', which has real but mixed support.
lead: Looksmatching is a term in looksmaxxing communities for couples whose members are rated as similarly attractive. Forum posts use it informally, for instance to remark that most of a group's couples were looksmatched.
claims: Most real-life couples are matched on looks.

name: Norwood scale
summary: The standard seven-stage chart for grading male pattern hair loss, used by clinicians and constantly by forums to size up a hairline and plan treatment.
lead: The Hamilton-Norwood scale, commonly called the Norwood scale, is a classification of male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) in seven main stages. It is widely used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons to describe severity, plan treatment and monitor change over time.

name: Facial symmetry theory
summary: The idea that more symmetrical faces are more attractive and signal good health; studies find a real but modest and context-dependent link, not a single decisive factor.
lead: Facial symmetry theory is the proposal that bilateral symmetry of the face makes it more attractive and that this preference reflects an evolved sensitivity to cues of health and developmental stability. Researchers distinguish fluctuating asymmetry, random left-right differences, from directional asymmetry, a consistent bias across a population.
claims: Facial symmetry is the main driver of attractiveness.
Fix symmetry first, before implants or fillers.
Symmetry only helps if the face also looks normal.
Asymmetry can be changed through posture or bone-related methods.

name: Dimorphism theory
summary: The idea that more sex-typical (masculine or feminine) facial features raise attractiveness; research on it is real but mixed.
lead: Dimorphism theory, in looksmaxxing usage, is the idea that facial and bodily differences between the sexes (sexual dimorphism) are central to perceived attractiveness, so that more strongly masculine male features and more strongly feminine female features are rated as better looking. It is a community framework rather than a single formal scientific theory, and it overlaps with academic work on facial masculinity and femininity.

name: Ascension
summary: Community term for a large improvement in one's looks over time; the word describes an outcome, not a specific method.
lead: Ascension is looksmaxxing community slang for a substantial improvement in a person's looks, and the verb ascend is used for someone undertaking one. Looksmax.org has many threads titled with the word, including plans, protocols with promised before-and-after photos, and long progress updates .
claims: A successful ascension is accompanied by strong emotion and reflection on one's past self.
Ascension does not fix psychological problems.

name: Hairstyle maxxing
summary: Choosing a cut and style to suit your face shape and hair type; cheap and reversible, with research showing hair shapes first impressions.
lead: Hairstyle maxxing refers to selecting hair length, cut and styling to improve overall appearance, particularly by matching style to face shape, forehead size and hair type. In forums the topic appears constantly as requests for hairstyle suggestions with photo posts, and members debate how much hair can compensate for other features .
claims: A good haircut can frame the face and hide flaws (the 'hair halo').
Hairstyle only helps if the underlying face is already attractive.

name: Color analysis
summary: Seasonal colour analysis: matching clothing and makeup palettes to skin undertone, hair and eyes; popular and low-risk, but little rigorous research backs its specific categories.
lead: Color analysis, usually called seasonal color analysis, is a system that advises people which colours to wear based on features such as skin tone, hair and eye colour. People are typically assigned to one of four seasons, winter, summer, spring or autumn, with winters and summers described as having blue undertones and springs and autumns yellow ones .

name: Voice maxxing
summary: Working on pitch, resonance and delivery to sound more attractive or masculine; speech-therapy techniques exist, but no trials test it for attractiveness.
lead: Voice-maxxing refers to deliberate changes to pitch, resonance, and speaking style, usually to sound deeper or more masculine, in order to be perceived as more attractive or authoritative. It is a common subtopic on looksmax.org, where threads ask whether a deep voice increases attractiveness and how much .
claims: A deep voice makes a man more attractive.
Women prefer higher-pitched voices, so a deep voice is a disadvantage.

name: Dripmaxxing / fashion
summary: Dressing and styling to look better; a low-cost softmax with no clinical research behind it.
lead: Dripmaxxing is the looksmaxxing-community term for improving one's appearance through clothing, accessories and styling rather than through changes to the face or body. "Drip" is internet and hip-hop slang for stylish dress, and the "-maxxing" suffix marks a deliberate effort to optimise it. Forum discussions typically cover outfit choice, fit, brands and the idea that dressing well can raise how attractive a person is perceived to be.

name: Beard maxxing
summary: Growing and shaping facial hair to frame the jaw; cheap and reversible, with mixed research on attractiveness.
lead: Beard maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of growing, shaping or enhancing facial hair to change how the lower face and jawline appear. Community members describe a beard as one of the cheapest and most visible changes a man can make, and discuss styles aimed at framing the jaw, disguising a weak chin or short ramus, or adding perceived masculinity .
claims: A beard is among the easiest, cheapest big looksmaxes
A beard only helps men with recessed or weak jaws; stubble is better otherwise
Patchy beards can be improved with minoxidil or transplants

name: Squintmaxxing
summary: Habitually narrowing the eyes for a "hunter" look; free, reversible and untested.
lead: Squintmaxxing is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person habitually narrows the eyelids slightly, aiming for the look community members call "hunter eyes": a lower upper eyelid line and a more intense, less wide-open gaze. Proponents describe it as a free, instant adjustment that can make the eye area look more attractive .
claims: A slight squint gives "hunter eyes" and a boost to appearance ratings
Squinting too much could harm the face or hair

name: Dental work / teeth maxxing
summary: Whitening and tidying teeth; peroxide products have trial support, with sensitivity as the usual trade-off.
lead: Teeth maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of improving the colour and look of the teeth, most often through whitening. Community discussion centres on whitening strips, toothpastes, dentist treatments and do-it-yourself methods, often alongside orthodontics and other dental work .
claims: Whitening strips and pastes are ineffective compared with a DIY method
Natural remedies such as coconut oil or baking soda whiten teeth

name: Hair dye / bleaching hair
summary: Dyeing or bleaching hair for colour and contrast; common cosmetic practice with documented allergy risk.
lead: Hair dyeing and bleaching change the colour of scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair with chemical colourants or lighteners. In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed as ways to adjust contrast, cover grey, darken sparse eyebrows or beard, or change overall look .
claims: Dye on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair improves how dark and full they look
Natural dyes are a safer alternative

name: Carrot maxxing
summary: Eating lots of carrots to tint the skin orange-gold; carotenemia is real but takes weeks and is a medical curiosity.
lead: Carrot maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of eating large amounts of carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden or orange tint. It relies on carotenemia (also called carotenosis), a documented, benign condition in which excess dietary carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layer .

name: Tyrosine supplements for tanning
summary: Amino-acid pills or lotion sold on the idea that more raw material means more melanin, with no human tanning trials behind it.
lead: Tyrosine supplements for tanning refers to the practice of taking L-tyrosine, a standard amino acid, as pills or applying it in lotions with the aim of darkening skin or speeding a tan. The idea rests on tyrosine's role as a building block of melanin, the pigment produced by melanocytes .

name: Baby oil tanning
summary: Oiling up to tan faster, a mid-century habit that adds no UV protection and has no studies behind its claimed benefit.
lead: Baby oil tanning is the practice of applying baby oil or similar oils to the skin before sun exposure, in the belief that it speeds or deepens a tan. Because such oils typically contain no sunscreen filter, the practice is associated with greater sunburn risk .
